options.text: All gray wolves living and interacting in Yellowstone National Park
options.why: They’re members of one species living and interacting in the same area, so they form a population.

options.text: All animals living in Yellowstone National Park
options.why: That includes many species. It’s part of a community rather than one population.

options.text: All organisms and abiotic conditions in Yellowstone National Park
options.why: That describes an ecosystem because it includes organisms and their abiotic environment.

options.text: All gray wolves living in separate habitats throughout the world
options.why: Members scattered across isolated areas don’t form one interacting, interbreeding group.

questions.stem: Why should quadrat locations be selected randomly?

options.text: To reduce systematic bias toward particular parts of the habitat
options.why: Random selection gives every possible location an equal chance and reduces the sampler’s influence on the result.

options.text: To guarantee that the estimate equals the true population size
options.why: Random sampling still produces sampling error. It reduces bias but can’t guarantee the exact value.

options.text: To ensure that every quadrat contains some members of the species
options.why: Empty quadrats are valid data. Avoiding them would bias the estimate toward areas where the species occurs.

options.text: To remove natural variation in abundance across the study area
options.why: Random sampling measures variation rather than removing it. Patchy distributions can still produce widely different counts.

questions.stem: Twenty-five 1 m² quadrats contain a mean of 8 plants. The habitat covers 500 m². What is the estimated population size?

options.text: 4,000 plants
options.why: The estimated density is 8 plants per square meter, so 8 × 500 gives 4,000 plants.

options.text: 200 plants
options.why: That multiplies the mean by the number of sampled quadrats. It estimates only the sampled area, not the 500 m² habitat.

options.text: 1,600 plants
options.why: That uses the habitat area divided by the sample count but fails to apply the mean density across the full area.

options.text: 62.5 plants
options.why: Dividing habitat area by mean count doesn’t scale population density to the size of the habitat.

questions.stem: Which conditions support a valid capture–mark–release–recapture estimate?

options.text: Marks persist, marked animals mix fully, and marking doesn’t alter capture probability
options.why: These conditions allow the proportion marked in the second sample to represent the proportion marked in the population.

options.text: Marks fade, marked animals remain together, and both samples have equal sizes
options.why: Faded marks and incomplete mixing reduce marked recaptures. The two sample sizes don’t need to be equal.

options.text: Immigration increases, marked animals avoid traps, and sampling occurs once
options.why: Immigration and trap avoidance break the assumptions, and the method requires an initial capture followed by recapture.

options.text: Births occur, marking improves survival, and marked animals stay near release sites
options.why: Population change, altered survival and incomplete mixing all make marked animals unrepresentative of the population.

questions.stem: Which factor is most clearly density-dependent?

options.text: Faster pathogen transmission in a crowded colony
options.why: Close contact becomes more frequent as density rises, so the pathogen’s effect changes with population density.

options.text: A volcanic eruption covering the colony in ash
options.why: The eruption can affect organisms regardless of how crowded the population was, so it’s density-independent.

options.text: An unusually severe winter freezing the colony
options.why: Low temperature can kill individuals at high or low population density, making it density-independent.

options.text: A flood removing the colony’s entire habitat
options.why: Habitat loss from the flood doesn’t become stronger because individuals are more crowded.

questions.stem: What pattern indicates exponential growth when population size is plotted on a logarithmic vertical axis against time?

options.text: An approximately straight rising line
options.why: Equal proportional increases occupy equal distances on a logarithmic axis, turning exponential growth into a straight-line pattern.

options.text: A horizontal line at carrying capacity
options.why: A horizontal line shows no net population growth, which fits a stable population rather than exponential increase.

options.text: An S-shaped curve that gradually levels off
options.why: That describes sigmoid growth on ordinary axes as density-dependent limits become stronger.

options.text: A repeating cycle with equally spaced peaks
options.why: Cycles can arise from changing interactions or conditions, but they aren’t the expected pattern for exponential growth.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a community from an ecosystem?

options.text: A community contains interacting organisms, while an ecosystem also includes abiotic conditions
options.why: The community is the living component. An ecosystem includes that community and its physical environment.

options.text: A community contains one species, while an ecosystem contains several species
options.why: One species in an area forms a population. A community already contains interacting organisms from multiple species.

options.text: A community contains producers, while an ecosystem contains consumers and decomposers
options.why: Producers, consumers and decomposers can all belong to the same community.

options.text: A community occupies one habitat, while an ecosystem always contains several habitats
options.why: The distinction concerns living and abiotic components, not a required number of habitats.

questions.stem: Which exchange occurs in the mutualism between hard corals and zooxanthellae?

options.text: Zooxanthellae provide photosynthetic products; corals provide carbon dioxide, nutrients and shelter
options.why: Each partner gains resources. The algae receive a protected habitat and raw materials, while the coral receives organic products.

options.text: Corals provide prey; zooxanthellae protect the corals by producing antibiotics
options.why: That describes neither partner’s main role. Zooxanthellae are photosynthetic and transfer organic products to the coral.

options.text: Zooxanthellae fix nitrogen; corals supply glucose inside root nodules
options.why: That mixes the coral relationship with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules.

options.text: Corals digest zooxanthellae; zooxanthellae gain transport to new habitats
options.why: Routine digestion would benefit the coral while harming the algae, so it wouldn’t describe their mutualism.

questions.stem: One plant grows better after a neighboring species is removed from a field plot. What can be concluded?

options.text: The result supports interspecific competition but doesn’t prove it by itself
options.why: Removing the neighbor and measuring a response provides evidence for competition, but the removal may also change other conditions.

options.text: The result proves that both species occupy identical ecological niches
options.why: Competition can involve one shared resource without the species having identical niches.

options.text: The result proves that the removed species was an invasive species
options.why: Competitive effects don’t establish whether a species was introduced, invasive or endemic.

options.text: The result shows that the two species have a mutualistic relationship
options.why: If one species improves after the other is removed, the observation fits competition better than mutualism.

questions.stem: A chi-squared test finds a significant association between the presence of two species. Which interpretation is valid?

options.text: Their distributions aren’t independent, but the cause requires further investigation
options.why: The test supports an association. It can’t identify competition or another biological mechanism as the cause.

options.text: The two species compete for the same resource at every sampling site
options.why: A statistical association doesn’t identify a shared resource or show that competition occurs at every site.

options.text: One species directly causes the distribution observed in the other species
options.why: Association alone doesn’t establish causation. Abiotic conditions or additional species may affect both distributions.

options.text: The observed and expected frequencies are effectively the same
options.why: A significant result means the difference between observed and expected frequencies is unlikely under the null hypothesis.

options.text: More wolves reduce elk abundance, allowing browsed plants to increase
options.why: The change begins with a higher-trophic-level consumer and moves down through lower trophic levels.

options.text: More mineral nutrients increase grass growth and then herbivore abundance
options.why: The change begins with resource supply at the base of the food chain, so it’s bottom-up control.

options.text: A drought reduces plant growth and then lowers herbivore abundance
options.why: The effect begins with reduced producer resources and passes upward, making it bottom-up control.

options.text: More phytoplankton supports larger zooplankton and fish populations
options.why: Greater food supply at a lower trophic level supports consumers above it, which is bottom-up control.

questions.stem: How are allelopathy and antibiotic secretion similar?

options.text: Both release chemicals that inhibit potential competitors
options.why: Plants can release allelopathic chemicals, while microorganisms can secrete antibiotics. Both interfere chemically with competitors.

options.text: Both involve consumers killing prey for food
options.why: That describes predation. Chemical inhibition can occur without the competitor being eaten.

options.text: Both benefit the affected organism and the chemical producer
options.why: That would be mutualism. The affected competitor is inhibited rather than helped.

options.text: Both increase competition by adding resources to the environment
options.why: The chemicals deter or inhibit competitors; they don’t work by increasing shared resource supplies.
